subject: What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?

messages.author: 70a6da99d25bf217
messages.subject: What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
parts:
I'm trying to estimate a large latent variable model using RStan. I'm getting several divergent transitions after warmup when performing estimation on simulated data and am trying to diagnose the problem using pairs() plots. 

I've looked at scatterplots between each parameter and lp__ using the pairs() function. Most divergent transitions occur below the diagonal, suggesting that the model needs to be reparameterized. But how can I tell which parameters are the source of sampling problems? None of the parameters appear significantly correlated with lp__.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
parts:
The pairs plot by default sets up two chains above the diagonal
and two chains below the diagonal. So all this is saying is that
they're happening on a subset of the chains. You want to see where
the divergences are at to see if you can learn anything.

The ideal pairs plot will look like a bunch of bulls-eyes of
independent unit-scaled posteriors. Anything that smacks of high
correlation or varying scales can be a problem for adaptation or
sampling.

- Bob

Agreed. This will be a key principle in our methodology guides.
We've been learning a lot of this ourselves as we go. Michael's
about to roll out some really great case studies later this week
or next week.
> Certainly, it's a technical manual and not a handbook, but that's a very, very intuitive rule to guide the modelling process: try to make all the parameters standarized and uncorrelated.

The Stan manual's going to be split into two parts:

1. the reference manual with the language spec and the functions doc

2. a revised user's guide that we'll publish with CRC and online
in HTML using bookdown (just like Hadley Wickham's Advanced R book)
(and also as a freely downloadable PDF---we're committed to keeping the
doc open)
> Maybe too obvios, but it's worth noting this is true for actual parameters to be estimated and not for transformed parameters, right?

Correct. Keep in mind that's on the unconstrained scale,
not the constrained scale. So if you have a parameter with
<lower = 0>, it's the log of the parameter. If you have
a covariance matrix, it's the Cholesky factor with log-transformed
diagonal. Unfortunately, you can't access that directly through
RStan because it can't get the transforms out from the language (yet).

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
parts:
On Monday, February 20, 2017 at 1:16:42 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The pairs plot by default sets up two chains above the diagonal
and two chains below the diagonal.  So all this is saying is that
they're happening on a subset of the chains.  You want to see where
the divergences are at to see if you can learn anything.

This hasn't been true for a couple of years. By default, the draws (across all chains) with below median accept_stat__ are below the diagonal and those with above median accept_stat__ are above the diagonal. If there are divergent transitions above the diagonal, those can usually be fixed with a higher adapt_delta. If they are below the diagonal, you can try increasing adapt_delta but oftentimes you have to adjust the model.

Ben

On Monday, February 20, 2017 at 4:44:46 PM UTC-5, David wrote:
Thanks for your response. I was wondering if there was other information I was suppose to glean from the pairs() plots. In particular, if the divergent transitions are below the diagonal how do I know what part of the model I need to adjust?

You want to look below the diagonal for weird shapes with non-constant variance, particularly funnels and the like. This often happens with variance parameters or hyperparameters. Sometimes specifying log = TRUE helps when some of the variables are strictly positive but get very close to zero.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
parts:
> On Feb 21, 2017, at 12:25 PM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi David,
>
> I often look at n_eff samples in the summary report. I reparameterize where the n_eff is low or change the distribution, from cauchy to student-t with nu = 4.
> Sometimes I use the inv_gamma distribution (but I fit the range values with fitdistrplus) R-package and give some extra to the variance.
> Sometimes applying the MATT trick does help too. I never figured out however, why there is this problem in my models.
> Thus I felt modeling is an art not only a science.

There are two different things going on here.

For computational efficiency and numerical stability, we'd like
the parameters to be independent in the posterior and unit scale.
Ideally without fat tails. Unit normal works well.

Of course, we can't get that, but often we can reparameterize to
get the same inferences with a better behaved posterior. The centered
parameterization is better when there's a lot of data and the non-centered
when there's less; better here is looking more like a standard normal.

The other issue is the statistical aspect of the model. Often we wind
up with posteriors that are inconsistent with our prior information. Often
we're vague about prior information, but there's enough data to make up
for it. When there's less data, there's much more prior sensitivity.
So we want to look at the posteriors to see if they make sense, and if
not, apply stronger priors so that the end-to-end inferences make sense.

Andrew's "folk theorem" ties these things together---misspecified models
(either in the prior or in the likelihood) are often also hard to fit.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
parts:
On Friday, February 24, 2017 at 9:03:41 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
It plots them in a separate color, I believe, but I'm
clearly not up to date on the pairs plot any more.  One of
the plots does this.  Then you can see if they're all in
the neck of a funnel or on one side of a banana-shaped
posterior, you can detect some problems.

- Bob

Yeah divergences are plotted in red and hitting max-treedepth is indicated with yellow. There is also a new ggplot2-based version of the pairs plot that I pretty much have ready to go (https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/pull/69). It will be released as part of the bayesplot package. The ggplot version will also give you more control over the appearance of the points indicating divergences and hitting max-treedepth (sometimes in the base R version they are hard to see).

On another note, the trace plots in the bayesplot package (the mcmc_trace function) allow you to add a rug plot that shows where the divergences occurred. This isn't always helpful, but it gives you a different way to look at the divergences that can complement what the pairs plot tells you. Here's a quick demonstration using rstanarm, but it works the same for models fit using rstan too: 

library("rstanarm")

fit <- stan_glm(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
  # next line to keep example fast and also ensure we get some divergences
                prior = hs(), iter = 400, adapt_delta = 0.8)

# extract draws using as.array (instead of as.matrix) to keep
# chains separate for traceplot
posterior <- as.array(fit)

library("bayesplot")

# grab divergences ('nuts_params' is a convenience function in bayesplot)
divs <- nuts_params(fit, pars = "divergent__")
mcmc_trace(posterior, pars = "sigma", divergences = divs)

This results in the plots in the attached png file.  

Jonah
